Gibeon
GIB-ee-un
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Gibe'on (H1391), "hill city" (from geva, "hill"). A Canaanite city north of Jerusalem whose inhabitants deceived Israel into a treaty (Josh 9). Distinct from Gibeah (Saul's town).

See also: Gibeon

📖 Biblical Definition

Gibeon was a prominent Canaanite city whose inhabitants, by a famous deception, secured a covenant of peace with Israel, and which became the scene of one of the great miracles of the conquest and the site of the tabernacle in David's day. When the Israelites entered Canaan, the Gibeonites, hearing of the destruction of Jericho and Ai, feared for their lives. Rather than fight, they resorted to cunning: they sent ambassadors in worn-out clothes with moldy bread, pretending to be travelers from a far country, and persuaded Joshua and the elders to make a covenant with them (Josh 9). The text records Israel's failure: "the men took of their victuals, and asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD" (Josh 9:14). When the deception was discovered three days later, Israel honored the oath they had sworn rather than break covenant, but made the Gibeonites "hewers of wood and drawers of water" for the house of God (Josh 9:21-27). The episode teaches the danger of acting without seeking the LORD's counsel, and the binding seriousness of a sworn oath even when obtained by deceit (centuries later, Saul's violation of this oath by killing Gibeonites brought a famine in David's day, 2 Sam 21). When the kings of the southern Canaanites attacked Gibeon for making peace with Israel, Joshua came to its defense, and the LORD fought for Israel, casting down great hailstones and causing the sun to stand still over Gibeon for about a whole day — "there was no day like that before it or after it" (Josh 10:11-14). Later, the tabernacle and the bronze altar stood at the high place of Gibeon (1 Chr 16:39; 21:29), and there the LORD appeared to the young King Solomon in a dream and granted his request for wisdom (1 Kings 3:4-15). Gibeon thus combines a lesson in the danger of prayerlessness, a testimony to the binding nature of covenant oaths, the memory of the sun standing still, and the place where Solomon received wisdom from God.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A Canaanite city whose people deceived Israel into a covenant (Josh 9 — "asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD"); scene of the sun standing still as the LORD fought for Israel (Josh 10:12-14); site of the tabernacle where God gave Solomon wisdom (1 Kings 3:4-15).

GIBEON, proper noun. Hebrew Gibe'on (H1391), "hill city"; a Canaanite city north of Jerusalem.

Its people deceived Joshua into a covenant by pretending to be from a far country (Josh 9).

Israel's failure: "the men... asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD" (Josh 9:14); yet they honored the sworn oath.

When attacked for making peace with Israel, Joshua defended it; the LORD fought, and the sun stood still over Gibeon (Josh 10:11-14).

The tabernacle and bronze altar stood at the high place of Gibeon (1 Chr 16:39); there God gave Solomon wisdom in a dream (1 Kings 3:4-15).

📖 Key Scripture

Joshua 9:14 — "And the men took of their victuals, and asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD."

Joshua 10:12-13 — "Then spake Joshua to the LORD... Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon. And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies."

1 Kings 3:5 — "In Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream by night: and God said, Ask what I shall give thee."

1 Kings 3:9 — "Give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Gibeon is corrupted when the lesson of prayerless decision is missed, when the binding force of the oath is dismissed as legalism, or when the sun-standing-still miracle is explained away rather than received as the LORD's mighty act for His people.

expand to see more

Prayerless-decision lesson missed. The heart of the Gibeon deception is Israel's failure stated plainly: "the men took of their victuals, and asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD" (Josh 9:14). They judged by appearances — the worn clothes, the moldy bread — and did not seek the LORD, and so were deceived into a covenant they would not have made. The lesson is permanent and searching: God's people are led into error not chiefly by the cunning of others but by their own failure to seek the LORD's counsel before acting. The remedy for being deceived is prayer; the cause of much trouble is the prayerlessness that trusts its own discernment of appearances.

Oath-binding dismissed. When the deception was discovered, Israel did not break the covenant, though it had been obtained by lies; they honored their sworn oath, because the name of the LORD had been invoked in it (Josh 9:19-20). Modern readers may find this strange — why keep an oath secured by fraud? The Scripture treats the sworn oath, taken in the LORD's name, as binding even at cost (Ps 15:4, "he that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not"), and the later famine that fell when Saul violated this very oath (2 Sam 21) shows how seriously God regards it. The episode rebukes a casual age that treats vows and oaths as disposable: a word sworn before God binds, and the LORD requires it to be kept.
